query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy nanoalloys, the balance between high configurational entropy and specific, favorable atomic pair interactions governs their structural and chemical stability at high temperatures. When the enthalpic attractions between certain element pairs (e.g., Al–Ni in an Al-containing system) become pronounced, they drive local chemical clustering (short‐range order) that can compromise the single-phase disordered state despite the overall entropy stabilization.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanocrystalline high-entropy alloy (e.g., an Al0.1CrCoFeNi system) synthesized to form a near-equimolar, random solid solution.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermal treatments, varying the dwell time or cooling rate at high temperatures close to the operating range, to allow or restrict atomic diffusion and local chemical ordering.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted at temperatures approaching a significant fraction of the alloy’s melting point (e.g., >0.8 Tm) under inert atmosphere; comparisons between rapidly quenched samples and those annealed for extended periods to promote equilibrium clustering.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical short-range order (SRO) manifested as elemental clustering (e.g., enhanced Al–Ni pairing) within the nanoscale alloy grains.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, rapid atomic vibrations favor disorder by maximizing configurational entropy; however, when particular pairwise enthalpic interactions are strong, they can locally overcome the entropy gain and produce short-range ordering. The competition between these opposing thermodynamic drivers—entropy favoring a homogeneous mix and enthalpy favoring specific cluster formation—determines the observed stability of the nanoalloy structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples processed with rapid quenching should maintain a largely random solid solution, ensuring structural stability and expected high-temperature properties. In contrast, samples subjected to extended annealing (or slower cooling) should display evidence of increased local chemical clustering, possibly accompanied by subtle changes in mechanical integrity or thermal behavior compared to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Rapidly quenched high-entropy nanoalloy with a nearly ideal disordered single-phase structure.
generation.boundary: The prediction is expected to hold for high-entropy nanoalloys in which the elemental constituents have similar atomic sizes but exhibit non-negligible differences in pairwise mixing enthalpies; the effect is most relevant near high operational temperatures (e.g., >0.8 Tm) and may vary with composition and processing history.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature or time threshold at which local clustering becomes significant is composition-dependent and may vary with differences in processing methods. Quantitative estimates of clustering extent and its impact on properties remain uncertain without further systematic investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy nanoalloy samples (e.g., Al0.1CrCoFeNi): one set rapidly quenched to freeze in the disordered state and another set annealed at high temperatures (close to the operating condition) for extended periods to allow potential atomic rearrangements. Characterize both sets using atom probe tomography (APT) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) to quantify the extent of local chemical ordering. Additionally, perform mechanical and thermal testing to detect any property changes linked with clustering.
measurements: Local chemical composition and clustering via APT.
Nanostructural imaging and identification of short-range order via HRTEM.
Mechanical property tests (e.g., nanoindentation, yield strength measurement).
Thermal stability assessment (e.g., differential scanning calorimetry, high-temperature XRD).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit statistically significant increases in local chemical short-range order or clustering relative to the rapidly quenched baseline, and there is no corresponding alteration in mechanical or thermal behavior, then the hypothesis that local pair-driven clustering governs high-temperature stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this report, we establish a force-field for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy and validate it by comparing structural properties, relative stability, and pair probabilities with first-principles calculations and limited experimental results. After the validation, we employ the new potential to investigate the large-scale deformation characteristics of Al0.1CrCoFeNi using atomistic MD simulations. Thus, we address the absence of well-developed force-field functions for high-entropy alloys and provide the EAM-LJ parameters to define the self- and cross-interactions of the participating elements in the alloy. In Al0.1CrCoFeNi, the electronic-structure-based linear-response calculations predict clustering driven by Al-Ni pair correlations (forcing Al-Al and Ni-Ni clustering behavior). The MD simulations are in agreement with the clustering trend, as given by the large clustering domains of like pairs dominated by Al-Al. Although an increase in temperature reduces the clustering strength of like pairs, Al-Al correlations still dominate. cited_evidence.text: Figure 2IIa shows the B2-BCC structural energy difference calculated from the RBA model plotted together with the FCC-BCC difference as a function of n. It is found from the RBA calculations that competition between the FCC and B2 phases starts at valence electron concentration, n ≈ 8. Comparison with the present experimental data for CCFN-Al0.5 (n = 7.67) where FCC peaks are indicated in XRD (Fig. IIc), shows that the RBA model may overestimate the stability of the B2 phase. However, in comparison with a new HEA composition, AlCoCrFeNi2.1, where the corresponding valence electron concentration is n = 7.70, the experimental observation of an FCC/B2 dual-phase constitution. Furthermore, experimental evidence of B2 presence has also been reported in CCFN-Al0.75, CCFN-Al1, and CCFN-Al1.5 with n values ranging from 6.57 to 7.41. These observations not only validate our theoretical prediction but also demonstrate that the formation of B2 phase is strongly correlated with the short-range chemical order between Al and the excess composition of Ni transition metals in the HEAs, suggesting possible effects of the processing method and cooling rate, as noted by Dahlborg et al..

Over last 15 years high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) have gained much appreciation for their numerous superior properties. In this paper we have shown a novel simulation methodology to realistically predict the nanometer level local structural features of complex Ta0.25Nb0.25Hf0.25Zr0.25 HEA. This involves prediction of the morphology of the short-range clustering (SRCs), their quantitative atomic composition at the nano level and the thermodynamic aspects. An alloy structure model containing 11664 atoms was created and this was subjected to structure evolution at 1800 °C. The structure evolution technique is based on a combined hybrid Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics (MC/MD) approach. The simulated results from this work are further validated against experiments and material characterizations reported in literature and done by high-resolution transmission electron micrograph (HRTEM) for the nano-level microstructure, atom probe tomography (APT) for the local chemical compositions and X-ray diffraction at synchrotron sources for the local lattice relaxation effects.
